headline: Self-Appointed Meme Fact-Checker Has Corrected 847 Joke Posts This Month
subheadline: Woman's commitment to accuracy extends to obviously satirical content, baffling internet
summary: A Threadit user has gained notoriety for leaving detailed fact-check comments on memes, jokes, and clearly satirical posts across multiple platforms.
content:
When someone posts a meme claiming cats have nine lives, most users scroll past or leave a laughing emoji. Brenda Whitmore leaves a three-paragraph correction with citations.

"Cats actually have one life, like all mammals," begins her most recent comment on a r/funny post. "The myth originates from cats' ability to survive falls and their flexible spine structure. See: Journal of Veterinary Science, 2019, Vol. 12."

The meme was a picture of a cat photoshopped onto a motorcycle with the caption "living his ninth life to the fullest."

Whitmore, 52, a retired reference librarian from Millbrook, has become something of an internet legend for her tireless dedication to correcting humorous content. Her post history reveals 847 fact-check comments in the past month alone, spanning Threadit, Chirper, VidTube comments, and even InstaSnap captions.

"Misinformation doesn't become acceptable just because it's formatted as a joke," Whitmore explained via email. "Someone might read that cats have nine lives and genuinely believe it. Then they let their cat do something dangerous. I'm preventing that."

Her corrections range from the pedantic to the genuinely educational. A viral post about historical inaccuracies in movies received a 2,000-word breakdown. A meme about sharks prompted a detailed explanation of marine biology. A joke tweet about coffee received links to three peer-reviewed studies on caffeine metabolism.

"She corrected my post about pizza being a vegetable," reported user @SarcasticSam. "It was clearly a joke about school lunch regulations. She wrote four paragraphs about nutritional classifications."

Whitmore's comments frequently receive more engagement than the original posts, though not always positively. Users have begun preemptively tagging her in obviously absurd content just to see her response.

"I've been told I don't understand jokes," Whitmore acknowledged. "I understand them perfectly. I simply don't think factual accuracy should be sacrificed for humor."

She recently expanded her operation, creating a Chirper account dedicated solely to meme corrections. It has 12,000 followers, roughly split between people who find her helpful and people who follow for entertainment.

"Someone has to do this work," she stated. "The internet has no editor. So I appointed myself."

Her most-liked correction to date: a detailed takedown of a meme claiming humans only use 10% of their brains. The meme had 847 shares. Her correction has 3,000.
author: Kevin Park, Internet Culture
